title: The global north: HIV epidemiology in high-income countries
paragraphs: Taking this to heart, the aim of the study from which this article derives was to provide insights into how gay men have become known and depicted within bureaucracy and public policy in Sweden-as well as its related "artefacts" [40,41]-with the discovery and outbreak of HIV. In many high-income countries, HIV is more prevalent among Men who have Sex with Men (MSM) than among the general population [42][43][44]. Through triangulation of crosschecking data from multiple sources [45], this article specifically looks at how gay men historically became associated with HIV in Sweden, and what this has meant for them as a sexual minority.

Thus, in summary, the early epoch in Sweden was distinguished by HIV and AIDS being seen as a relatively defined and limited problem [34,68,[71][72][73] that would solve itself without any interference. This would explain the political decision of not 'combating' the potential epidemic with nothing but limited resources and inputs [74,75]-which is not to be considered characteristic of Sweden, but rather, something archetypical of Western Europe altogether [44,74,[76][77][78]. This consensus changed, however, in February 1985, when a young boy suffering from haemophilia contracted HIV from a unit of blood plasma given to him at a Swedish hospital.
